cards.title: Introduction to ORM and JPA
cards.content:
Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) bridges the gap between object-oriented programming (Java) and relational databases (SQL).

JPA (Jakarta Persistence API) is a specification (a set of interfaces and rules), while Hibernate is the most common implementation of this specification.

cards.title: What is Spring Data JPA?
cards.content:
Spring Data JPA is a part of the umbrella Spring Data project. It makes it easy to implement JPA-based repositories.

Instead of writing boilerplate EntityManager code and transaction management manually, Spring Data JPA allows you to simply define repository interfaces, and it generates the implementations automatically at runtime.

cards.title: Entity Mapping Basics
cards.content:
An entity represents a table in your database. Every entity class must be annotated with @Entity and have a primary key marked with @Id.

@Entity
public class User {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    
    @Column(name = "user_name", nullable = false)
    private String username;
}

content.question: Which annotation is used to specify that a Java class represents a database table in JPA?

cards.title: Repository Interfaces hierarchy
cards.content:
Spring Data JPA provides built-in interfaces to handle common CRUD operations:

  • Repository: The base marker interface.
  • CrudRepository: Provides basic CRUD operations (save, findById, delete).
  • PagingAndSortingRepository: Adds pagination and sorting capabilities.
  • JpaRepository: Combines all of the above plus JPA-specific operations like flushing the persistence context and deleting in batches.

cards.title: Derived Query Methods
cards.content:
One of the most powerful features of Spring Data JPA is the ability to derive queries directly from method names.

Spring parses the method name and automatically creates the SQL query. For example:

List<User> findByEmailAddressAndLastName(String emailAddress, String lastName);

It supports operators like Like, Between, LessThan, GreaterThan, and Containing.

content.instruction: Order the steps Spring Data JPA takes to execute a derived query method at runtime:

items.text: Spring parses the repository method name (e.g., findByEmail).
Spring translates the method name into an abstract JPQL query representation.
Hibernate compiles JPQL into database-specific SQL dialect.
Spring binds the method arguments to the SQL statement parameters.
SQL is executed on the database, and JDBC ResultSet is mapped back to Entity objects.

cards.title: Custom Queries with @Query
cards.content:
When derived query methods become too complex, use the @Query annotation. It supports both JPQL (default) and native SQL queries.

// JPQL (deals with Entity classes and fields)
@Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.status = :status")
List<User> findByStatus(@Param("status") String status);

// Native SQL (deals with actual tables and columns)
@Query(value = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE status = ?1", nativeQuery = true)
List<User> findByStatusNative(String status);

content.instruction: Match each feature to its corresponding query type:

pairs.value: Operates directly on Java Entities and object properties
Operates on physical database tables and column names
JPQL automatically adapts to different database dialects
Native SQL is ideal for accessing non-standard database extensions

cards.title: Pagination and Sorting
cards.content:
To prevent performance issues when querying large tables, use pagination. Spring Data JPA makes this simple by accepting a Pageable parameter and returning a Page or Slice.

Pageable pageable = PageRequest.of(0, 10, Sort.by("username").descending());
Page<User> usersPage = userRepository.findAll(pageable);

Page returns the requested data plus the total count of matching records (requires an extra SQL count query).

content.question: What is the primary performance advantage of returning Slice instead of Page?

options.text: Slice does not trigger an extra count query to the database, which is faster for large datasets.
Slice automatically compresses the data returned over the network.
Slice does not support sorting, making execution simpler.
Slice allows you to bypass transactional boundaries.

cards.title: Transaction Management
cards.content:
Database operations must be performed within transaction boundaries to ensure consistency (ACID properties).

Use the Spring Framework's @Transactional annotation on your service classes or methods. Spring Data JPA's built-in repository methods (like save() or delete()) are transactional by default.

cards.title: Auditing in Spring Data JPA
cards.content:
Auditing allows you to automatically track metadata like who created or modified an entity and when.

By adding @EnableJpaAuditing to your configuration, you can use annotations inside your entities:

  • @CreatedDate: Captures when the entity was created.
  • @LastModifiedDate: Captures when the entity was last updated.
  • @CreatedBy: Captures who created the entity (integrates with Spring Security).

cards.title: Summary & Best Practices
cards.content:
Congratulations! You've learned the core tenets of Spring Data JPA:

  • Define entities with @Entity and @Id
  • Extend JpaRepository for instant CRUD
  • Leverage Derived Queries and custom @Query when needed
  • Implement Pagination with Pageable to safeguard performance
  • Protect data integrity using @Transactional
